skill.name: structured-logging
skill.description: Guides agents to write structured logging with wide events, canonical log lines, and query-friendly context for production debugging.
skill.summary: Design wide structured log events that make production debugging easier.
skill.author: Chemiseblanc

security_audit.summary: The static external command, sensitive file, and reconnaissance alerts are false positives caused by Markdown formatting, observability field names, and defensive guidance. No prompt injection or executable behavior was found. One medium semantic issue remains because the logging guidance can encourage broad collection of user, payment, business, and infrastructure data.

remediation.suggestion: Add explicit minimization rules for user identifiers, email, permissions, payment last four, business values, and retention windows.
Mark host, pod, container, node, deployment, and git fields as internal-only and redact them from customer-facing logs.

remediation.issue: Markdown false positives in static scanning
remediation.suggestion: Label pseudocode and query fences clearly as examples so automated scanners can separate documentation from executable commands.

semantic_findings.title: Overbroad Sensitive Data Logging Guidance
semantic_findings.description: The skill recommends logging broad user, business, payment, and infrastructure fields. It warns against unnecessary PII, but it should add stronger redaction and minimization rules.

content.value_statement: Scattered logs make production incidents slow to diagnose. This skill guides Claude, Codex, and Claude Code to design wide events with actionable request context.
actual_capabilities: Explains one wide event per request per service.
Lists fields for request, user, business, error, timing, infrastructure, and feature flag context.
Shows examples of scattered logs and improved wide events.
Provides middleware-style pseudocode for building and emitting events.
Demonstrates queries that analyze failures, latency, and user segments.
limitations: Does not include executable tooling, tests, or logging library integrations.
Examples are pseudocode and must be adapted to each stack.
Sensitive field guidance needs local privacy, retention, and redaction review.
Does not configure log storage, dashboards, or alerting.

use_cases.title: Add Canonical Request Logs
use_cases.description: Create a single request completion event with timing, status, user, and business context.

use_cases.title: Improve Incident Investigation
use_cases.description: Identify fields that help compare failures by customer tier, feature flag, error type, and latency.

use_cases.title: Review Logging Standards
use_cases.description: Evaluate existing log statements against wide event practices and remove scattered low-context messages.

prompt_templates.title: Plan a Wide Event
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner: design fields before writing logging code.
prompt_templates.prompt: Help me design one wide event for this request flow. Include request, user, business, error, timing, and feature flag fields. Flag sensitive fields that need redaction.

prompt_templates.title: Improve Existing Logs
prompt_templates.scenario: Intermediate: convert scattered messages into one event.
prompt_templates.prompt: Review these current log statements and propose a single canonical log line. Preserve useful context, remove duplication, and explain any privacy concerns.

prompt_templates.title: Add Middleware Logging
prompt_templates.prompt: Design a middleware logging pattern for this service. Show where to initialize context, enrich it, handle errors, and emit the final event.

prompt_templates.title: Audit Observability Coverage
prompt_templates.prompt: Audit this service for structured logging gaps. Compare the current fields with wide event guidance, identify missing dimensions, and prioritize changes by incident value.

output_examples.input: A checkout service logs payment retry messages across several statements.
output: Replace the scattered messages with one request completion event.
Keep payment provider, attempt count, latency, final error type, and retry result.
Redact payment details and avoid storing full card or token values.

output_examples.input: A database timeout log only says that the query failed.
output: Add request identifier, operation name, table, timeout value, elapsed time, and rows scanned.
Include the user segment only when allowed by policy.
Add a suggested remediation that helps the responder act quickly.

output_examples.input: An API team wants to query slow enterprise requests.
output: Capture duration, status code, endpoint, subscription tier, trace identifier, and relevant feature flags.
Use consistent field names so incidents can be filtered across services.

best_practices: Define redaction rules before adding high-cardinality user fields.
Emit one complete event at request completion instead of many partial messages.
Use consistent field names and types across services.
anti_patterns: Do not log raw tokens, passwords, full card numbers, or unnecessary PII.
Do not split one request story across many unconnected log lines.
Do not rely only on low-cardinality messages like failed or timeout.

faq.question: What is a wide event?
faq.answer: A wide event is one structured log entry with many useful fields about a request or operation.

faq.question: Does this skill run commands?
faq.answer: No. It is documentation and guidance for designing structured logs.

faq.question: Can I use it with any logging library?
faq.answer: Yes, but you must adapt the examples to your language, framework, and logging backend.

faq.question: How does it help debugging?
faq.answer: It keeps request, user, timing, error, and business context together so incidents are easier to query.

faq.question: Should I log user data?
faq.answer: Only log user data that is necessary, approved, and protected by redaction and retention controls.

faq.question: Does it replace tracing or metrics?
faq.answer: No. It complements traces and metrics by adding rich event context for investigation.
